strengths: The dataset addresses a useful extension of RVOS: paired expressions and separate masks for interacting entities. Its 8,738 clips and 127,314 expressions cover appearance, motion, multiple instances, and actor–target relationships, offering potential value beyond the proposed model.

Cross-dataset results substantiate the usefulness of the training data. With comparable expression counts, InterRVOS-5K improves Sa2VA over Ref-SAV from 32.8 to 41.8 on MeViS valid, 54.2 to 61.8 on Ref-Youtube-VOS, and 62.1 to 67.1 on Ref-DAVIS (Tables 3 and A2).

Joint segmentation provides meaningful gains on the proposed benchmark: ReVIOSa-1B improves overall J&F from 53.8 to 59.7 and the interaction subset from 58.9 to 69.8 over Sa2VA-1B. Table 6 also supports joint supervision over independently supervised role tokens.
The supplementary material provides detailed annotation prompts, dataset statistics, and qualitative examples, making the language-generation pipeline relatively transparent.
weaknesses: The provenance and reliability of the segmentation ground truth are not established. The pipeline starts with highlighted object masks but never explains how dense mask tracks are obtained from VidOR, whose standard object annotations are bounding-box tracks. Neither mask-generation procedures nor quantitative mask-quality checks are reported. This is a consequential omission for a segmentation benchmark, affecting both reproducibility and confidence in its scores.

The automatically generated benchmark lacks an independent annotation-quality audit. There are no measured rates for interaction correctness, referent ambiguity, or expression–mask alignment, including on the evaluation set. Examples such as 'Person explaining to person and car' (Figure A2) illustrate why fluent generation and prompt-level self-checking alone cannot establish reliable interaction labels.

The quantitative evaluation does not clearly establish the central capability of correctly segmenting both roles from one expression. Section 5.2 describes standard J&F restricted to paired interaction expressions, without specifying how both output masks are scored, how missing or swapped roles are penalized, or how single-output baselines are adapted. Separate role scores or a joint pair-success measure are absent, leaving the dual-output claim supported mainly by qualitative examples.

The claimed semantic roles are inconsistent with the annotations. Sections 4.2–4.3 describe the actor as the acting entity, but Figure A1 labels the child in 'child being assisted by man' as the actor; Figure A2 similarly labels the car being worked on as the actor. The implementation appears to distinguish the referred subject from other participants, rather than consistently identify agent and recipient roles. This materially weakens the interpretation as actor–target reasoning.

The causal claim that interaction modeling produces broader understanding exceeds the evidence. The dataset changes source domain, caption diversity, and supervision together, without isolating interaction annotations. Moreover, Table A2 shows ReVIOSa underperforming Sa2VA trained on the same data on MeViS valid, Ref-Youtube-VOS, and Ref-DAVIS. Architecture details also omit the token-generation loss, optimization settings, and handling of multiple target instances. The demonstrated gains are worthwhile, but the unresolved benchmark-validity and evaluation issues currently outweigh them.

strengths: The proposed task addresses a useful extension of RVOS: segmenting multiple interacting entities from one expression. Complementary descriptions and explicit entity associations could support research on relational video grounding.

InterRVOS-8K provides substantial scale and expression diversity: 8,738 clips, 35,247 objects, and 127,314 expressions, including motion-only and multi-instance references. The appendix provides annotation prompts, dataset statistics, and illustrative examples.

The dataset's usefulness is supported beyond its own evaluation set. With the same Sa2VA baseline, InterRVOS-5K improves zero-shot J&F over Ref-SAV from 32.8 to 41.8 on MeViS valid, 54.2 to 61.8 on Ref-Youtube-VOS, and 62.1 to 67.1 on Ref-DAVIS (Table A2). These are meaningful transfer gains.

Joint segmentation supervision has promising empirical support. ReVIOSa-1B improves overall J&F from 53.8 to 59.7 and interaction-subset J&F from 58.9 to 69.8 over Sa2VA-1B (Table 5). Table 6 also shows a substantial advantage over independently supervised role tokens.
weaknesses: The central dataset contribution lacks essential ground-truth documentation and validation. The pipeline explains expression generation but does not explain how the segmentation mask tracks were obtained from the VidOR source, prompted, propagated, or verified. Neither the main text nor appendix reports a human audit or quantified accuracy for masks, expression grounding, or interaction labels. Because the evaluation annotations are also automatically constructed, this leaves benchmark reliability materially uncertain.

The quantitative evaluation does not clearly establish the proposed single-expression, dual-output capability. Section 4.3 describes scoring the referred entity through [SEG_ACT], while Section 5.2 defines Actor-Target evaluation primarily as restricting standard J&F to paired interaction expressions. The manuscript does not specify how both outputs from one expression are scored, how conventional single-output baselines are adapted, or whether complementary expressions must produce consistent entity assignments. Table 5 therefore supports improved segmentation on relational expressions more directly than successful joint actor-target reasoning.

The role definitions conflict with the annotations. Section 4 describes the actor as the acting entity and the target as the affected entity, but Figure A1 labels the child as Actor in 'child being assisted by man'; Figure A2 similarly labels the car as Actor in 'Car being worked on by person.' These examples appear to encode grammatical subject versus other participants rather than stable semantic actor-target roles. This affects the claimed task semantics and supervision, beyond terminology alone.

The experiments do not isolate interaction reasoning as the source of improvement. ReVIOSa mainly extends an existing MLLM–SAM2 framework with two segmentation tokens and additional mask supervision. Table 6 supports joint supervision, but does not distinguish relational learning from the benefit of supervising an additional entity. Likewise, dataset comparisons change motion, multi-instance, and interaction content together. Table A2 also shows ReVIOSa below the same-data baseline on MeViS valid, Ref-Youtube-VOS, and Ref-DAVIS, limiting claims of broadly improved video understanding.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied prompts. Appendix A omits learning rates, optimizer details, frame sampling, loss weights, and the language-generation training objective; baseline training configurations and evaluation filtering rules are insufficiently specified. These omissions are secondary to the benchmark-validity concerns, but complicate verification. Overall, the demonstrated transfer gains and useful task direction are worthwhile, yet uncertainty about ground-truth quality and whether the evaluation measures the central claimed capability currently favors weak rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful extension of RVOS: segmenting multiple interacting entities with explicit role assignments. Complementary expressions and joint segmentation provide a meaningful direction beyond conventional single-referent evaluation.
InterRVOS-8K is substantial: 8,738 video clips, 35,247 objects, and 127,314 expressions, including motion-only and multi-instance descriptions. The detailed annotation prompts improve transparency.

The strongest evidence concerns dataset usefulness. With the same Sa2VA baseline, InterRVOS-5K improves zero-shot MeViS valid performance from 32.8 to 41.8 over Ref-SAV training (Table 3). Table A2 also reports gains on Ref-Youtube-VOS and Ref-DAVIS, supporting value beyond the proposed benchmark.

Joint supervision produces promising improvements. ReVIOSa-1B achieves 59.7 overall J&F versus 53.8 for Sa2VA-1B, and 69.8 versus 58.9 on interaction expressions (Table 5). Table 6 supports joint prediction over independently supervised role tokens.
weaknesses: The segmentation ground truth is insufficiently documented. The dataset originates from VidOR, whose standard object annotations are bounding-box trajectories, but the four-stage pipeline describes expression generation and assumes masks already exist. The manuscript does not explain how dense masks were obtained, propagated, or validated. This is a material reproducibility and benchmark-validity concern.

There is no reported independent annotation-quality audit, including for the evaluation set. Claims of high-quality interaction descriptions rely on generation prompts and examples, without measured expression correctness, referent uniqueness, role accuracy, or mask quality. For a primarily automatic dataset contribution, these omissions leave the reliability of the central resource uncertain.

The actor-target evaluation does not clearly establish joint segmentation accuracy. Section 5.2 describes standard J&F restricted to paired interaction expressions, but does not specify how both outputs from one expression are scored or how single-output baselines are adapted. Separate target-mask results, pair-level success, and role-swap consistency are absent. Consequently, Table 5 supports improved segmentation on interaction expressions more clearly than successful joint interaction understanding.

Semantic roles are inconsistent with the stated task definition. Sections 4.2–4.3 describe the actor as the acting entity and the target as the affected entity, yet Figure A1 labels the child in 'child being assisted by man' as Actor, and Figure A2 labels 'Car being worked on by person' as Actor. The labels appear to follow the grammatical referent rather than stable interaction roles. This affects supervision and the interpretation of role-aware reasoning, beyond terminology alone.

The architectural contribution is a modest extension of segmentation-token prompting, and the mechanism behind the gains is not isolated. Joint prediction adds mask supervision; Table 6 does not establish whether improvements require explicit role semantics rather than generic additional-entity supervision. Broader architectural generalization is also mixed: Table A2 shows ReVIOSa below the same-data Sa2VA baseline on MeViS valid, Ref-Youtube-VOS, and Ref-DAVIS.

Despite worthwhile transfer results, the missing mask-construction procedure, unmeasured annotation reliability, and underspecified joint evaluation concern the paper's central contribution. These material uncertainties outweigh the current evidence for acceptance; the recommendation is not driven by limited benchmark breadth or minor presentation issues.

strengths: The task addresses a useful limitation of conventional RVOS: separately grounding both participants in a described interaction. Role-specific masks could support video relationship understanding and downstream activity analysis.

InterRVOS-127K is a substantial resource: 8,738 clips, 35,247 objects, and 127,236 expressions, including 17,604 actor–target expressions (Table A4). The four-stage annotation pipeline is explained with detailed prompts, and the evaluation expressions and masks are reported to receive human correction.

The reported segmentation improvements are meaningful. ReVIOSa-1B improves over Sa2VA-1B from 57.0 to 62.0 J&F on the dataset’s RVOS evaluation and from 71.3 to 73.3 on interaction actors. Table 4 provides a useful factorial ablation showing contributions from both AML and the dual-token formulation.

The supplementary transfer experiments strengthen the dataset contribution beyond its own benchmark. In Table A3, training the Sa2VA baseline on InterRVOS improves zero-shot results over Ref-SAV and ReVOS across the reported benchmarks. Table A2 also shows benefits with smaller expression subsets.
weaknesses: The central semantic-role definition conflicts with the annotations. The paper motivates actor and target as the initiator and receiver of an asymmetric interaction, but Figure A6 labels the child as actor in 'child being assisted by man' and reverses the labels for 'Man helping a child.' Figure A7 similarly labels the car as actor in 'Car being worked on by person.' These examples follow grammatical reference rather than invariant interaction roles. This is consequential for a task whose principal novelty is semantic role asymmetry: the benchmark does not clearly distinguish subject/complement grounding from identifying who acts on whom.

The evaluation does not establish an advantage over straightforward alternatives for the new task. Table 2 contains no competing target-segmentation results, although existing models could be adapted using separate actor/target queries or two ordered segmentation tokens. Table 4 reports only aggregate RVOS scores, without actor/target ablations or role-confusion measurements. Consequently, the evidence supports better segmentation but does not isolate the claimed improvement in interaction understanding from additional mask supervision and ordinary multi-entity grounding.

Dataset validity is insufficiently documented for a benchmark-centered contribution. Human correction is stated, but annotation instructions, auditing results, agreement, and residual expression/mask error rates are absent. Some illustrated expressions are questionable, including 'dish feeding person and child' in Figure A10 and 'Person explaining to person and car' in Figure A7. Appendix D.3 creates multiple clips per source video without specifying whether source videos are disjoint across training and evaluation. This leaves evaluation independence unverified; it does not establish that leakage occurred.

AML needs a more precise mathematical specification. Equation 6 applies binary cross-entropy directly to softmax attention weights and binary foreground masks. An attention row has total mass one, so multiple foreground entries cannot simultaneously approach the target value one. This can still function as an attention-concentration regularizer, but it differs from the stated mask-alignment interpretation. Any rescaling or normalization is unspecified, and the AML weight is not reported, making the actual optimization difficult to reproduce.

Reproducibility and attribution remain incomplete despite the extensive appendix: learning rate, optimizer, LoRA configuration, sampled-frame count, loss weights, baseline training protocols, and the data used for head selection are not specified. The architecture combines established MLLM-to-SAM prompting with role tokens and attention supervision, so the dataset and controlled interaction evaluation carry much of the contribution. The useful transfer results favor the work, but the unresolved task semantics and missing direct comparisons on its defining capability currently make the balance favor rejection.

strengths: Separately segmenting both participants in a language-described video interaction is a useful extension of RVOS. InterRVOS-127K provides substantial infrastructure: 127,236 expressions over 8,738 clips, including 17,604 actor–target interaction expressions, with human refinement of evaluation expressions and masks.

The dataset has demonstrated transfer value beyond its own benchmark. In Table A2, training Sa2VA on InterRVOS-28K yields 40.2 zero-shot J&F on MeViS valid versus 32.8 using Ref-SAV's 72K expressions. Table A3 also supports the usefulness of the dataset across three established benchmarks.

The architectural ablation provides evidence that both proposed components help segmentation. Table 4 improves from 57.0 to 58.5 with AML, to 59.6 with interaction tokens, and to 62.0 with both. Table 2 also reports stronger actor segmentation than the listed baselines.

The supplement provides extensive annotation prompts, dataset examples, attention visualizations, and additional benchmark results. These make the pipeline substantially more inspectable than the main paper alone.
weaknesses: The central semantic-role claim conflicts with the supplied annotations. Figure A6 labels the child as actor in 'child being assisted by man,' while labeling the man as actor in 'Man helping a child'; Figure A7 similarly labels the car as actor in 'Car being worked on by person.' These examples track the grammatical subject or primary referent rather than a stable interaction initiator. This can define a useful grounding task, but it does not establish the claimed distinction between semantic actor and recipient. The discrepancy affects the interpretation of the benchmark and its claimed interaction understanding, rather than merely terminology.

The new task lacks a meaningful comparative evaluation of target segmentation. Every baseline's InterRVOS-Target entry in Table 2 is absent. An adapted multi-output baseline or two role-specific queries to an existing RVOS model would help establish whether the proposed architecture improves on straightforward solutions. Table 4 reports only the aggregate RVOS score, without actor/target breakdowns or role-confusion measurements. Consequently, the evidence supports improved segmentation more clearly than improved role discrimination; additional target supervision and architectural changes are also bundled in the token ablation.

Important benchmark-validity details remain unspecified. Although evaluation annotations are reportedly corrected by humans, the manuscript gives no annotation agreement, audit results, correction rates, or interaction-expression counts by split. Appendix D.3 extracts multiple clips from source videos but does not establish source-video-disjoint training and evaluation splits. This does not demonstrate leakage, but leaves independence unverifiable. Figure A7's 'Person explaining to person and car' also illustrates why a systematic audit of generated interaction semantics matters.

AML's mathematical specification needs clarification. Equation 6 applies BCE directly between normalized attention weights and a binary foreground mask. Attention weights share a unit probability budget across keys, whereas a mask may contain many positive patches; therefore, the attention map cannot match the stated binary target. Such a loss can still encourage foreground attention, but any rescaling, normalization, and reduction are material to reproducing and interpreting it. Loss weights, learning rate, frame sampling, and the data used for head selection are also unspecified. The main text describes a LLaVA-based backbone, whereas Appendix A identifies InternVL-2.5.

The broader results do not isolate the claimed benefit of modeling inter-object dynamics. Appendix C.1 explicitly evaluates an AML-only variant on standard benchmarks, so Table A1 primarily supports attention supervision. The dataset-transfer comparisons are valuable but do not separate interaction annotations from differences in source videos, motion descriptions, or other annotation content. Overall, the dataset and segmentation gains are worthwhile, but the unresolved task semantics and absence of competitive evaluation on the defining two-role task make the current balance favor weak rejection.

strengths: Separately segmenting the two entities in a referring interaction is a useful extension of RVOS. The dataset and evaluation protocol could support research beyond single-object grounding.

InterRVOS-127K provides 127,236 expressions over 8,738 clips, including 17,604 actor–target expressions. Human correction of evaluation expressions and masks is valuable, and the appendix supplies detailed annotation prompts.

Table 2 demonstrates meaningful improvements: ReVIOSa-4B achieves 74.5 actor J&F and 64.5 overall RVOS J&F, versus 71.0 and 59.5 for Sa2VA-4B. Table 4 supports complementary benefits from dual-token supervision and AML, improving the 1B baseline from 57.0 to 62.0.

Cross-dataset experiments strengthen the dataset contribution. In Table A2, training Sa2VA on the 28K-expression subset yields 40.2 zero-shot MeViS J&F versus 32.8 using Ref-SAV's 72K expressions. These transfer results provide evidence of usefulness beyond the proposed benchmark.
weaknesses: The role definition conflicts with the semantic interpretation motivating the task. Figure A6 labels the child as actor in 'child being assisted by man,' while labeling the man as actor for the same event expressed as 'Man helping a child.' Thus, labels follow the referred grammatical subject rather than consistently identifying the action initiator. This does not invalidate paired grounding, but materially weakens claims about learning semantic actor–target directionality.

The central target-segmentation capability lacks a comparative baseline: every competing method has a dash in Table 2's target columns. Evaluating existing RVOS models with separate actor/target prompts, or an adapted two-output baseline, would establish whether specialized tokens improve interaction grounding beyond ordinary entity grounding. Table 4 reports aggregate RVOS performance rather than target performance or role-confusion rates, leaving that distinction unresolved.

Dataset quality and benchmark construction are insufficiently audited. The manuscript reports human refinement but gives no correction rates, annotation agreement, or quantitative assessment of generated interaction labels. Appendix D.3 describes extracting multiple clips per source video without explicitly establishing source-video-disjoint splits. These are consequential uncertainties for a dataset-centered contribution, rather than evidence that leakage occurred.

AML is underspecified mathematically and operationally. Equation 6 applies binary cross-entropy directly to softmax attention weights and binary masks; those weights share a probability budget and cannot simultaneously approach one across multiple foreground patches. The objective can still concentrate attention, but its interpretation and any rescaling need clarification. Loss weights, learning rate, LoRA configuration, frame sampling, and the data used for head selection are also missing.

Overall, the useful dataset, consistent local gains, and transfer evidence balance against unresolved questions about the task's semantic interpretation and the absence of comparative evidence for its defining capability. This places the manuscript at the acceptance boundary; the reservations concern central claims, not merely presentation or failure to lead every benchmark.
